statement: A student proposed implementing the lock through the network: a server that accepts only one connection at a time, so whichever consumer grabs the connection holds the lock and others are rejected or wait.
detail: The student imagined a protocol that accepts only one connection and rejects others, with the queue broadcasting to subscribers who then compete for the port. The teacher called it a good, brilliant idea.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I was thinking on network perspective. So one thing came to my mind was port.

statement: A single-connection lock can be built as a normal TCP server: instead of accepting connections in a loop and handing each to a thread, the server accepts one connection and handles it, so only one client (process) can be connected until the first has finished processing.
detail: The teacher tied it to the load balancer code walked through earlier, which makes it easy to see how to do it over the network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So normal TCP connection or is a normal TCP server that you can set up to get this done. Only one client can connect.

statement: If a consumer holding a single-connection lock dies, its TCP connection goes down and the server (queue) knows the connection is gone, which releases the lock naturally.
detail: The teacher did not explicitly confirm; he answered that it can be implemented but that he could not fully evaluate it in two minutes.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: The consumer dies then because the consumer dies, the TCP goes down, right? If it dies also connection is gone.

statement: The student had held back the network idea because the queue had been declared a black box exposing only library APIs; leveraging the network itself for locking sidesteps that.

statement: The single-connection lock idea is valued because it is fundamental and out-of-the-box: the lock is simply preventing others from connecting; writing such a server is an easy implementation that can be done within a few hours, and the teacher encouraged doing it.

statement: Some real queues (a student cited OCI's queue) hide a message from other consumers as soon as one consumer receives it (visibility off); that is specific to those queues and not part of the lecture's example.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: immediately it sets like no visibility to off so that other consumers cannot even see the message in queue.

statement: The queue in the remote-lock example is deliberately hypothetical and gives zero protection: any consumer that asks just gets the message. It was chosen as a constraint to understand remote locks, not as a design to re-architect real systems around.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a hypothetical zero protection. That's what I was saying. It gives you zero protection over here.

statement: Real queues such as RabbitMQ, SQS and Kafka give the guarantee that a message is not handed to multiple consumers, so you do not have to build anything around it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you talk about RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka and whatnot, they give you this guarantee. So you don't have to do anything around it.

statement: Nothing connects Redis to the queue in the example; the protection works because we write the consumer code ourselves, and that code first gets the lock and then reads the message - that is the problem statement.
detail: A student objected that a consumer could read from the queue without acquiring the lock; the teacher's answer: without the lock the same message can go to multiple consumers, which is what we want to avoid.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's our consumer, our logic. We are writing it, right? So you would write it first, get the lock, then read the message.
flags: check: "So why should there be?" may be the Teacher

statement: Where remote locks are used: a MongoDB distributed transaction updating three documents on shards one, three and five holds locks on those documents; another transaction wanting the same documents must wait. That lock information must be stored somewhere shared - a remote lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine MongoDB distributed transaction across multiple shards.

statement: MongoDB gives these guarantees via its own lock manager that records which transaction holds a lock on which document of which shard; a second transaction asking for a locked document is told to wait until the first commits or rolls back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what MongoDB does is it gives you those guarantees, but how it is implementing it, it is having its own lock manager

statement: The queue example is the same pattern: three consumers contend for a shared resource and we track locks so only one moves forward - effectively a distributed transaction using Redis as the lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We just implemented a distributed transaction where we are using Redis as a lock.

statement: To synchronize two entities, look for the nearest storage they share: two threads share RAM (mutex, semaphore); two processes have separate RAM so the disk is shared; two machines share an external database - anything over a network.
detail: A student summarized this principle; the teacher replied "Excellent. Anything over a network."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if we try to synchronize two different entities, then we always try to look for the nearest shared storage system.

statement: Synchronizing two independent distributed systems (e.g. two clusters doing heterogeneous work) is still multiple machines on a common network, so the same approach - a shared store over the network such as Redis or a database - applies.
detail: The teacher first pushed back that "distributed system" is a very vague term.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But it's still network is common between them, right? They're all part of the same network.
flags: check: speaker of "Let's say we want to target a machine..." (Teacher?) at 02:46:31

statement: When multiple machines are involved, synchronization is always over the network: the network is the only thing shared between machines, neither RAM nor disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Network is the only thing that is shared between machines, neither RAM nor disk.

statement: Storing a TTL with the lock bounds how long a process can hold it, but every implementation has this limit; without it you run the bigger risk of perpetual locking, where a lock (or consumed message) is never deleted and the entire system stalls.
detail: A student asked whether the TTL becomes a bottleneck since a process can then run for at most that time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single implementation has it. Otherwise you are running a bigger risk of perpetual locking.

statement: A student thought implementing a mutex would be harder than a network lock; the teacher corrected that a mutex is two lines of code in C, because everything is in memory in a single RAM and coordinating threads is peanuts.
detail: Correction: the mutex is in-memory, single-RAM, thread-level coordination.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Implementing mutex is two lines of code in C. That's it.

statement: Network communication is much more costly than in-memory signalling - the worst mode of communication; a mutex's in-memory signalling is peanuts for the operating system, so prefer signalling over network calls any day.
detail: The student argued the network lock just polls rather than signals; the teacher pointed to how many network calls the polling loop makes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, network is much more costly any day. It's the worst mode of communication.

statement: If the critical section is on one single server (not remote), use the normal local primitives - synchronized, a mutex, atomic instructions; Redis is not needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can use normal synchronized.
flags: unclear: "May if you rapid use mutex"

statement: Redlock edge case raised by a student: a client acquires locks on three of five Redis instances, then two of those instances go down; when nodes come back, another client can acquire a majority, so two clients hold the lock on the same resource.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: After the lock acquired, two instances go down, so effectively has taken only one

statement: This is exactly the known Redlock edge case: Redlock is not foolproof, it only minimizes the chances - what are the chances that the servers holding your locks go down?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is not a full proof, but it still minimizes the chances.

statement: In Redlock, a client that fails to acquire the lock on a majority of instances releases the locks it did acquire.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If I was not able to acquire the lock on all instances, like majority of locks, what I would do? I would release...

statement: Because losers keep releasing while the majority holder (C1) keeps trying to acquire the remaining instances, the system eventually converges to C1 holding the lock on all instances; only a majority is needed to move forward.
detail: Example with consumers C1-C4: C2 releases its two locks; C3/C4 may grab them but release too, while C1 also tries the third and fifth shards and eventually succeeds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So eventually your system will converge into the fact that on all the instances C1 would have the locks

statement: If lock-holding instances go down, a client still looping for a majority sees only three instances; one option is a global state saying the cluster is unhealthy and waiting for two more nodes to come up; otherwise it proceeds with a majority of what remains - and that is where it may wrongly think it holds the lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you may have a global state which says that, hey, my, my, my cluster is unhealthy, let's wait for two more nodes

statement: The edge case needs the two instances on which the majority holder already has the lock to go down before it acquires the remaining two - a window of hardly two or three seconds - so its probability is very low.
detail: The teacher is confident because other processes, failing to get more than 50%, keep acquiring and releasing, while C1 keeps trying the remaining instances.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for it to acquire lock on these two, it would hardly take two or three seconds, not more than that.

statement: A client that already holds a majority still keeps trying to acquire the lock on the remaining instances, because that minimizes (not covers) the edge case.
detail: A student asked why C1 would try M2 when it already has a majority.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So to cover the edge case, C1 is allowed to minimize, not cover, to minimize, right?

statement: Test distributed behaviour by simulating it: put heavy load on the system and inject explicit delays (one second, five seconds, 15 seconds) to mimic edge cases and watch how the system reacts.
detail: The teacher says he can explain Redlock confidently because he implemented and mimicked this situation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I typically simulate the situations with delays that one second delay, five second delay, 15 second delay in order to mimic this situation

statement: You do not need multiple machines to study distributed systems: the teacher ran five Redis instances on his local machine on ports 6379, 6380, 6381, 6382 and 6383 to mimic Redlock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instances of Redis running in my local machine 6379, 6380, 6381, 6382, 6383. That's it.

statement: Distributed-system edge cases are minimized, never claimed fully covered or fully mitigated; the one line people miss (keep trying the remaining instances / release on failure) is the line that makes all the difference.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These edge cases are minimal. We never say it is fully covered. We never say it is fully mitigated. Minimized.

statement: System design and distributed systems are not just theoretical and need no fancy infrastructure: read research papers and always implement them, going in depth on the edge cases where things falter and mimicking them with explicit delays (e.g. run five processes instead of five servers).
detail: Prompted by a student noticing the pattern of papers plus implementation across three weeks; the load balancer is the classic example of something intimidating that becomes easy once implemented.

statement: ZooKeeper-based locking does exactly what was built with Redis; you either implement it with Redis or use ZooKeeper.

verbatim: It does exactly what I talk about. Exactly this. So either you implement with Redis or do you use ZooKeeper.

statement: A student argued ZooKeeper gives more guarantees (persistent leader, fewer time/expiry/network problems); the teacher replied you can add persistence to the Redis approach too, and that he is not saying it is better than ZooKeeper, only another implementation.
speaker: teacher

statement: As an engineer you need to know how a tool like ZooKeeper is implemented internally, not just say "use ZooKeeper".

statement: In the load balancer design, the Redis Pub/Sub used to push config changes can be replaced by ZooKeeper: ZooKeeper has a distributed config store that notifies everyone when something is updated - internally it needs a persistent connection on which updates are broadcast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what we talk about is Redis Pub/Sub. You can replace it with ZooKeeper, right?

statement: ZooKeeper's notification framework is just real-time Pub/Sub: it maintains a pool of TCP connections and, when something changes, notifies everyone subscribed - exactly what Redis Pub/Sub did in the design, so the system would work fine with either.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ZooKeeper's notification framework is just real-time Pub/Sub. That's literally what it does.

statement: Many young organizations and startups stay away from ZooKeeper: they associate it with Java (most startups are not on Java), find it intimidating, and are more comfortable building a scrappy solution on Redis.

statement: DNS does not route to another load balancer when one is loaded: it just holds the mapping of a domain to multiple IP addresses and round-robins between them, with no information about load.

statement: For active-passive load balancers, DNS holds only the active load balancer's IP address; alternatively use weighted round robin with weight 0 for the passive one and 1 for the active one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: IP address will only contain active load balancer IP address.

statement: The orchestrator knows the IP addresses of all LB servers and when one goes down or comes back, so it is the orchestrator that updates DNS - not a manual step.

statement: For session handling across multiple servers, route a user's requests to the same server with consistent hashing in the load balancer rather than adding a separate session service, which would add a network hop.

statement: Do not add services (random boxes) to a design for the sake of it: every service is a network hop that slows things down; unless there is a very good justification, find the shortest path possible.

statement: Every network call adds roughly three to five to 10 milliseconds of latency; at scale teams optimize even every microsecond and challenge every single network hop.
speaker: teacher

statement: Redis Pub/Sub is used for broadcasting config changes to the LB servers because it gives real-time sending to everyone out of the box, whereas otherwise the process would have to make multiple calls to every server; any real-time broadcast mechanism (server-sent events, ZooKeeper, explicit HTTP calls) would work.

statement: A student proposed running three orchestrators with the same code, the rest idle until one fails; the teacher refined it: not idle - leader-follower.

statement: The orchestrator would be a single point of failure; going down is not fine. The fix is leader-follower: one master, followers doing grunt work (not idle), and if the master goes down a follower automatically takes its place with one or two seconds of downtime - leader election.

statement: Every component of the load balancer design is highly available: backend clusters via autoscaling, LB servers, the database, the orchestrator via leader election, and CoreDNS via leader election.

statement: Autoscaling is a separate service in the design (as AWS has a separate autoscaling service) because customers configure scaling policies through their own admin UI; the orchestrator watches and scales LB servers, and backend scaling can be done by the orchestrator per autoscaling policies or by a separate component.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: AWS has a separate autoscaling thing.

statement: Whether autoscaling is its own component depends on how bulky the orchestrator becomes: if very bulky, separate it; otherwise let the orchestrator read autoscaling policies from a DB and scale backend servers. A component is needed anyway to accept developers' policy configuration endpoints.

statement: Nothing autoscales the orchestrator: it runs in multi-node mode (one master, multiple followers) with leader election, so if the master goes down a follower takes over and the orchestrator as a whole never goes down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is a leader election. So, so if master goes down, one of the leader, one of the followers would do about it

statement: Like any infrastructure, there is always a global monitoring service (Prometheus-like) watching all VMs and key components, including the master orchestrators; it has its own leader and minimal duties - check each master and react if something goes down - and a standby keeps its own failure probability low.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there would always be a global monitoring service, something that is taking care of all, that is monitoring all the VMs out there

statement: The global monitor is the base condition of the recursion: an orchestrator for the orchestrators that monitors their master nodes, triggers leader election or adds worker nodes - and it is final because its responsibilities are very minimal.
speaker: teacher
